After 5 long public years of trial, error and experimentation from the devs, It's finally here, and having beaten the game twice and getting P rank on all of the first floor levels, I can say this game more than lived up to my expectations. 

If you've heard about this game before, you've probably heard it be compared to the Wario Land games, and that's a pretty big deal for some since Wario has been absent from platforming games since Wario Land: Shake it 2008. For a bit of context, a big part of what really made the Wario Land games click was their emphasis on controlling a complex 2D character in simple, exploration based environments designed to let the player let loose with their moves. Pizza Tower not only understands what made these games good but expands on it and carves out it's own identity due it it's increased emphasis on movement and score attack mechanics. Peppino has a dizzying amount of moves that can at first make him feel sloppy and bloated to play, but his moveset is designed to be chained together and the levels allow you to make the most of his moveset. It makes it very cathartic to master Peppino and the levels you have him fly through.

This is all coupled with an absolute back to back banger OST, top notch visual presentation, and a fantastic cast of characters making for a game I'll be replaying again and again for years.
It's pretty rare to be able to declare the Game of the Year this early in the year

Pizza Tower is a game I highly recommend.

Not because it's the best platformer I've played in years.

Not because the soundtrack slaps harder than an overtuned spanking machine. (Seriously, it's probably my favorite since Deltarune & Undertale.)

Not because of the incredible art style.

Not even because of the fact that this game deserves to succeed because of the sheer effort and dedication shown by the development crew.

I recommend Pizza Tower because of the character arc, even though all of the preceding points are completely valid reasons to recommend it. Peppino is not a greedy treasure hunter like Wario. He is not a successful and heroic plumber like Mario. He is not.. uh, Luigi. Peppino is a small business owner being antagonized by a bigger, stronger competitor he can't possibly financially threaten, and he knows it. 

Throughout the entire game, it is very clear he knows it; everything about Peppino's body language is designed to convey one simple message - this guy is as highly strung as a freshly-tuned violin atop the Empire State building. This makes him easy to relate to for most people living in the 21st century. Unless the player is a level-die gamer, your journey through the Pizza Tower will almost certainly see poor Peppino subjected to violent abuse, both mental and physical. The archetypes of a nervous chef and a victimized small business owner are further combined with the sympathy you should naturally feel for Peppino when he gets beaten down by the Tower because of your own fuckups.

All of this makes it that much more satisfying when Peppino finally snaps.

"What did he mean by this?" I'm not going to tell you. This is an answer you'll need to find for yourself. Play Pizza Tower.

I'll be honest... I am not the best guy at video games.  
It took me 100 hours to 100% the entirety of Pizza Tower. Achievements, P rankings, (all except for saving Snotty, RIP boy).   
I have never 100%-ed a game until now, because again, I am not the best guy at video games. I can't S rank Cuphead, the final levels of Rayman Origins had me frustrated, Dark Souls chewed my balls up.  

 But still I sat myself down and decided to spend 100 hours completing the entirety of Pizza Tower. I liked that. I liked doing it. I feel like I'm confessing some sort of crime. But after being conditioned by this game's frantic energy, the only crime I can think of is that I didn't do it faster.

I absolutely recommend it. Starting out, it is very intense and you will feel sloppy getting the hang of the movement. (I nearly refunded the game, so glad I didn't.) If there is a spark there for you and you're willing to stick with it and learn how to move more purposefully, you will see how much careful thought has gone into this game. Not just the hilarious art and music, I also mean the design and flow. I really can't think of many nagging issues the developers overlooked, it's all damn solid. Even pressing the windows key is a smooth experience! So many games overlook that and make it a struggle to look at your desktop. No issues here!) Whether you play Pizza Tower and go in bee-lining for the ending, or play with the intent to squeeze everything possible out of the game, I wish you the best of luck and quick reflexes.

Pizza Tower. No it’s not a metroidvania, rather it’s a new genre a Sonicoidario.

In essence, if someone asks me, “what is your favorite Wario game?” I’ll say “Pizza Tower.”If someone asks me, “what is your favorite Sonic game?” I’ll say “Pizza Tower.” If someone asks me, “what is your favorite Metroid game?” I’ll say “Pizza Tower.” You get the idea.

I did not expect to have a shine spark style move in a game where you play as a pizza chef climbing a doomsday tower controlled by the horror pizza villain from that one episode of Jimmy Neutrons more fever dream induced cousin, but it feels amazing. 

In a game centered on pizza, it plays as smooth as butter, no, better, like a garlic butter dipping sauce. I have been playing on the Steam Deck, and although it’s yet to be “verified,” I can’t imagine it running any better on another device.

Typically when a game gets Overwhelmingly Positive reviews on Steam, it's for one of two reasons. One reason is that the game does something radically new and attracts all sorts of attention. Baba Is You is a great example.

The other reason is that the game does something old, just really, [i]really[/i] well. Pizza Tower falls firmly into this category.

Pizza Tower doesn't do anything groundbreaking. It's a simple speed-based platformer. But every part of it has been polished dozens of times over. Every level is built to allow you to zoom through large swathes of it at great speed, but not so easily that it's trivial. When you manage to keep high speed through several rooms in a row, it just feels [i]really good[/i].

What I absolutely love about this game is how fluid and responsive the movement system is.  There were times that I tore through a section of level that I hadn't seen before, just to look back and go "What the fuck did I just do???" followed by a rush of serotonin.

And the music...dear god the music.  It's a crime that this OST didn't win any awards.
This especially becomes apparent if one were to attempt to 'P-rank' a stage, by hitting all 3 secrets, all toppings, and hitting the infamous Lap 2.  The music does a COMPLETE 180 from 'Hurry, RUN FOR YOUR LIFE' to an anthem of pure bravado, DARING death to catch you if it can.  You went into that pizza portal knowing EXACTLY what it meant and now you're either about to completely style on Pizza Face or else you're going to pay dearly for your arrogance.  

Even if you don't go that far into '100%'ing this game, there's so much zany funny shit to see.  When you've got a game that's basically Warioland with a Ren and Stimpy type of style, you KNOW you're in for a good time.

Get.  This.  Game.  It's worth it.

Writing this review after seeing Pizza Tower get screwed out of an award it rightly deserved - this game is probably my singleplayer game of the year for 2023. Tight controls that when learned facilitate some of the most satisfying high-speed movement I have ever experienced in any platformer, levels with satisfying layouts and gimmicks that make coming back to discover every little detail, P-rank them, do it again, and then do it with mods that add even more laps, nothing but fun all the way through. Bosses that're fun to fight against and avoid sugarcoating until you can defeat them without taking a single hit; an artstyle that's absolute eyecandy to look at, and a soundtrack that must have aimbot since it never misses to match, which provide a steady stream of enjoyment and nostalgia for '90s and 2000s cartoons and internet animation in tandem with the gameplay. It's not often that I call a game outright perfect, and I suppose nothing is perfect, but I'd say this game's extremely close, especially after patches that helped deal with the few rough edges that remained when the game initially launched; this is a game that I can see myself coming back to constantly for years to come, and is a game I can endorse wholeheartedly whether you're a casual player looking for a solid platformer to pick up and enjoy at your own pace, or someone that's willing to dump hundreds of hours into the game to do insane things some can only dream of.

I never followed the development of Pizza Tower. The game popped out at me on steam's new release section with its ridiculous name and wonderfully expressive art-style. Something about it stuck in my brain and eventually I had to try it.

Before playing this game I had no idea what a 'Wario-like' platformer even was. I've played Super Meat Boy, Shovel Knight, Hollow Knight and all kinds of mario and metroid style platformers my whole life, so for the first hour or so of Pizza Tower I was at a loss on how exactly I was even supposed to play this game. You CAN play it slowly and methodically, Mario style, precision jumping and getting through the level, but the game's level design is beckoning you, urging you to use Peppino's insanely intuitive and varied moveset to do something more.

Then it clicked.

The soundtrack, the visuals, the movement, the level design: all of it in perfect, insane, breakneck harmony. 19 levels doesn't sound like a lot, but every single one is so meticulously crafted, brilliantly unique, and urging you to push yourself to the limits of what you can do with its systems and layout that you can easily play each one dozens of times before reaching P rank. Each room feels like its asking you to do it a bit quicker, a bit more fluid, with more finesse. The game rewards you with ranks, points and achievements, but there is no bigger dopamine hit then when you are in the flow-state that this game can evoke, slamming through levels so fast your brain can barely process what you're seeing, but it does, it just barely does. In Pizza Tower, momentum, control and finesse are everything, and it has been honed over 5 years to pinpoint precision. Everything about the game is merely the vehicle for you to express yourself as this super-sonic, balding, middle aged PTSD riddled Pizza Man: Peppino Spaghetti.

[h1][b]A slice of heaven[/b][/h1]

Indie games come in many shapes and sizes, but many are made with the idea of being a modern take or spiritual successor on a classic game. Both [i]Shovel Knight[/i] and [i]Hollow Knight[/i], for example, are modern takes on [i]Mega Man[/i] and [i]Metroid[/i] respectively. [i]Pizza Tower,[/i] a successor to [i]Wario Land 4[/i] in particular is no different. I have not played the game it takes from, but I can still say with a great deal of confidence that this grease-covered gem has charged its way straight into the upper echelon of this niche, an echelon that arguably surpasses its inspiration.  

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

Visually, this game is an assault on the eyes in the best way possible. It's sort of like [i]Cruelty Squad[/i] in the sense that some of the initial learning curve is just processing what you see on the screen. However, I don't think [i]Pizza Tower[/i] has an ugly visual style, rather it's just chaotic and messy - again, in the best way possible. The art style is best described as 90's Nickelodeon cartoons like [i]Ren & Stimpy[/i] and [i]Rocko's Modern Life[/i] in a MS Paint format. I adore the aesthetic, and think they captured that surreal, geometric look perfectly with this game, and it fits the unabashedly and comically insane feel this game goes for. 

In addition, the animations in this game are astonishingly good. Everything is incredibly fluid and expressive. There's so many blink-and-you'll-miss-it moments, for example seeing the basic enemies become startled and wide-eyed at the sight of an anxious Italian man surpassing Usain Bolt's top speed charging right at them. 

Is it a Pillar John of art style and animation in games? Probably not, but this is a pie that knows a thing or two about presentation, and it does that point very well.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

This being a platformer, nailing the movement is key, and anxious greaseball Peppino controls remarkably well. For as overwhelming as this game can be, Peppino's moveset is both varied and tight. It takes some time to understand how to control peak Italian athleticism, but it feels immensely satisfying to master. Going fast is fun, and far more engaging than the high speeds of Sonic's preferences for autopilot. While you certainly will accidentally launch Peppino into a wall and kill your momentum at least twice per level, the game revels in its chaos. Like many a fast food joint, [i]Pizza Tower[/i] does not demand perfection, it demands efficiency. Getting the highly-desired P rank isn't obtained by making zero mistakes, it's done by embracing the breakneck rhythm the game sets its tempo at and finding the most efficient routes possible to maintain your combos. As an authentic meatbag that can't keep up with some of the robotic reaction times of some players, it's refreshing to play something that embraces the odd mistake if you can quickly get back into the fray.

While combat is rarely a priority, the bosses are a highlight. They test your skills in unique and interesting ways, and despite their challenge, were consistently fair in their mechanics and expectations. The final boss, in particular, was incredibly fun to fight and one of my favorite final bosses of recent memory. 

The level design is also a major highlight, and lends itself well to the "efficiency over perfection" approach. The core idea remains the same: Grab the Toppins, destroy Pillar John, get out quickly. However, each level has a very distinct identity, both visually and mechanically, and provides unique power ups befitting the thematic identity of the level. These are usually nice breaks in the gameplay, and they generally adhere to the core idea of moving fast. However, a few of the gimmicks did feel rather undercooked in their uses or how they controlled. It's not a significant issue, but for how polished the rest of the core gameplay feels, I did find it noticeable enough to leave a slightly underwhelmed taste.

I think another point [i]Pizza Tower[/i] can struggle with is in its difficulty. It's not too hard, just erratic in its expectations from level to level. I found a handful in the earlier stages of the game were more difficult than most of the later levels, even after I returned to them near the end with a greater familiarity of the mechanics and the level layouts. The game frontloads everything into its initial tutorial, which is fitting, but I still wish it did a better job of gradually introducing those mechanics. I can see this point being a turn-off for some players, which is unfortunate because I think the game's level design only gets better as you progress.

However, the game largely excels in what it sets out to do. It's fast, it's tight, and it's fair. Does it play better than [i]Wario Land 4?[/i] Frankly, I have no idea, but I can tell you it's probably the best [i]Sonic[/i] game I've ever played. 

[h1]Story[/h1]

I don't think the story is worth considering in the rating of this game. [i]Pizza Tower[/i] is a gameplay-focused experience that draws you in with its aesthetics, and it knows that. As such, the story is in the backseat and there isn't really much to talk about, other than it being present.

[h1]Audio[/h1]

While your taste buds may not get the satisfaction they're looking for when playing this game, your eardrums certainly will. I think the sound effects perfectly fit the cartoon aesthetic. I'm especially fond of the taunt sound effect, both as a parry and on its own. The former has a "pow" effect that makes parrying feel satisfying, while the horn sound that plays in both makes it thoroughly enjoyable to spam.

The music, however, is the real star of the show here. It's playful, upbeat, and catchy, but there's also a remarkable amount of depth here. For example, the secret levels have a groovy, percussive backtrack that sets the surreal tone of the level, but each secret level has a different melody corresponding with the original level you found the secret in, which blew my leitmotif-loving mind. "It's Pizza Time" is the best track, as it perfectly encapsulates the panic of having to escape from a level, and the final boss theme is also a treat, not mentioning the Waters of Nazareth-esque track from a late-game level.

[h1]Content Value[/h1]

[i]Pizza Tower[/i] takes somewhere around 6 hours to finish for a regular playthrough. However, levels are highly replayable and filled to the brim with secrets and hidden routes. While I did not go out of my way to P-Rank every level, it's definitely an appealing challenge that can easily inflate your playtime. While the game itself is pretty short, there's lots of side content and replay value to warrant the price tag.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

This game and [i]Wario Land 4[/i] go together like pineapples on pizza. Some people will look at this strange creation and find it repulsive, but the garlic-scented freaks like myself that give it a taste will have their senses enlightened by a chaotic barrage of exciting flavors and mechanics. You do not need an attachment to this game's inspiration to appreciate it for the absolutely stellar title that it is, so I highly recommend smelling the garlic and giving this eccentric gem a shot because of that. Even with its impressive polish, [i]Pizza Tower[/i] isn't quite the perfect pie for me, but don't let its minor shortcomings deter you, it's still remarkably close. Just remember, if you hurt Peppino too much, you can go to hell.

Legit one of the best platformers I've ever played. It was inspired by the Wario Land games, but, in my opinion, it far surpasses them. Every level introduces new and fun mechanics and themes, so the game stays fresh all the way to the end. The levels are designed for speedrunning, but you can also just play through them casually. Learning each level to achieve a perfect score seemed daunting at first, but it turned out to be very doable and a super fun experience. The soundtrack is also 10/10.

So, cards on the table right now, are you a Wario Land fan, and more specifically, Wario Land 4? That’s not exactly an all-star Nintendo franchise of course, owing to its unfortunate dormant state right now, but I imagine the answer for a lot of you would be ‘yes’. In that case, this is basically that but with a lot more pizza, and you’ll probably like it.

But I probably shouldn’t say one paragraph for a review, and in any case I have a lot to say about this game, since I do really like the Wario Land games and Wario in general. It would also be a bit unfair to describe Pizza Tower in such simple terms, because if any homage could ascend to being a great game on its own, this smashed right through the ceiling at Mach 5 (which is something you can do in-game). 

You play as Peppino Spaghetti, owner of a local pizza place down on his luck, probably because he built his restaurant on the edge of a cliff in the middle of nowhere. His day gets just a little worse when he’s suddenly accosted by Pizzaface, a floating pizza who declares he’s going to put Peppino’s business out of its misery with a giant laser. Someone has to go, and since Pizzaface’s restaurant is a five-story tower full of monsters, death-traps and gimmicks, you have your work cut out for you.

Gameplay in Pizza Tower is straight-forward, but also with a lot of depth. Each level tasks you with heading to the end by jumping and running like any platformer, whereupon you smack a load-bearing (and living) pillar out of the way…and discover that’s not the end, it’s the midway point. The real exit is the same door you entered from, which you now have to run back to under a time limit. Let it reach zero and Pizzaface pops in to chase you, and he’s a one-hit kill - the only thing in the actual levels capable of killing you, in fact. This means each stage has two halves: one more exploration and puzzle-focused, the other all action, with you frequently running through areas unique to the escape sequence that emphasize this. That said, it’s definitely possible to pilot Peppino very quickly through both halves if you know what you’re doing, since he can go very fast and controls equally well.

You may want to slow down a bit, though, since there are things to collect while you’re going through stages. Each level has five Toppins, little waddling pizza ingredients, imprisoned around it, and you’ll want to collect at least most of them since they give you money which you need to unlock the boss of each floor. Breaking through walls or exploring other paths during Pizza Time also lets you find three secret areas featuring Kickstarter backer cameos. Lastly each level has Gerome, the tower’s janitor, hanging around somewhere; bringing him to a particular door unlocks a treasure. 

Beyond progressing through the game and the thrill of finding them, these both give you score in the levels which affect your rank at the end of it, starting from D and heading up. Unless you’re deliberately not picking up items you’ll probably at least get a B, and finding all of the above virtually guarantees an A. Beyond that is where things get tricky, since most levels don’t give enough points to get a higher ranking…at least if you’re only doing it normally. 

After you’ve beaten a level and made it back to the exit door on a second try, you might notice a portal nearby reading ‘Lap Two’, which does exactly what it sounds like: hop in and you’ll receive a huge point bonus, at the cost of having to do the escape sequence a second time without anything extra added to the timer. You generally have to do this for an S-Rank unless you’re playing perfectly, and even then you’ll probably still need the extra points.

That’s an S for Perfect - but there’s a difference between calling something Perfect and it really being Perfect, isn’t there? If you beat the level doing all of the above, get enough points for an S-Rank and most importantly, start a combo in the first screen and sustain it the whole level, you get a P-Rank, signifying that you’ve completely mastered that stage in every regard. It won’t be lying either, since in order to do this you need to know everything there is to know about a given level. If you attempt one it might seem impossible at first, even in the early stages, but as you learn what Peppino can do and pick up on parts of the stage that let you keep your speed and momentum, it’ll quickly become a much more reasonable challenge.

Speaking of the stages, there are quite a few, and all are memorable in their own right. Almost no theme is repeated, and they run the gamut from typical video game locales to things that are a bit more out there - though even the former tend to be pretty inventive regardless. There are little touches that can make you smile, and numerous transformations that also don’t get old and add to your momentum in unique ways. This is all helped along by the animation, which was rather brilliantly modeled after classic cartoons from the 90s: every character has hugely exaggerated, sometimes deranged expressions, and Peppino has a ton of in-between frames or little touches for almost every motion you can have him do, like a one-second double take if he happens to fall off a platform while he’s turning mid-run. It’s honestly a treat.

More than any references or homages to other things, though, it feels like what makes Pizza Tower a truly memorable experience is that the developers obviously understood how to make a game that was. There’s almost no downtime as you play, with every level giving you something new to do. What story is in the game has a clear arc and a satisfying payoff. The music is great all-around, but contains recurring leitmotifs that are pleasant to listen to, something not every game does. There are reasons I wouldn’t recommend Pizza Tower, but they’re mostly subjective things, like not being into platformers or just not jiving with the aesthetic or inspirations. If it sounds like you would enjoy it, you probably will, even if you don’t have a slice handy.

Just remember, though: if you hurt Peppino too much, you can go to hell!

There's a reason this game is being hyped and praised by the people who've played it. If you loved Wario Land 4 or A Hat in Time: Seal the Deal challenges in particular, this game is hand tailored for you.

So what does this game get right?

-The first and most important thing is that the controls are just right for this type of game and just right for satisfying adrenaline junkies. This is a game that understands that the problem with modern Sonic games is that Sonic plays the game FOR you and you don't need to touch a button, whilst also understanding how more complex key combinations can lead to frustration and "speed bumps" that slow players down or make some players want to abandon a challenge entirely, as it ceases to be fun for them. The result is a control scheme that feels very fluid, making sections of the game you thought impossible feel like a breeze once you get the hang of it. 

I would be quick to point out for example that while it is true people might complain about Peppino doing things they didn't want him to do, I would say this is moreso a side effect of the necessities of the system in play, and the trade-off is 100000% worth it. Peppino can, if given an incorrect input, quickly chain this into a number of undesired actions that quickly run out of control for the player's combo, but the payoff is Peppino has exceptional mobility and control once one understands how he moves.

A basic example: if Peppino runs at a straight wall with no incline leading to it, he will crash into it and full stop. If however you grab an enemy near said wall and the grab animation leads Peppino and the enemy into the wall, this will cause Peppino to grab the wall once he's killed the enemy and start climbing it on his own without pause. This affords for quicker, smoother and unbroken runs through levels, but Peppino grabbing the wall over this difference might surprise and throw off new players.

Or as another: if Peppino is climbing a wall and you want to jump off it in the opposite direction, you simply hit the jump button. No directional, no nothing. Just one jump button press per wall jump you want. This initially seems counter-intuitive to what we as gamers might expect, but this is a control scheme you'll come to appreciate when Peppino rapidly needs to pivot between two opposing walls to navigate a level. It's beautifully simplistic, but yes of course it will also trip up new players when they mess up one of their wall jumps and this breaks the entire chain. Tying this back into the above example, if a new player doesn't understand the enemy-grab-into-wall will cause Peppino to start climbing the wall once the enemy dies, they'll hit the jump button in hopes of attaching him to the wall to make him climb it, but because he's already on doing so on his own, he'll jump off it in the opposite direction, which the player doesn't want.

However, these are not cases where one gets frustrated and thinks "bad controls," but rather you realize for this game to function well and for Peppino to be able to speed through levels as masterfully as he's capable, the inputs NEED to be simplistic or partially "on autopilot" so that it's possible for the player to keep up with it's pacing. This means the only hurdles with the controls are more about initially understanding how Peppino functions, and once you figure this out, it's a system that somehow manages to simultaneously feel satisfying, simplistic, challenging and rewarding all at once. The controls are FILLED with shortcuts, but until you realize which shortcuts exist, you'll trip up over them. Fantastic control scheme, but needs to be learned like any other.

-The soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal. I remember hearing early versions of the songs when the game was in the early stages of development and didn't find them too great, but somehow they refined the entire album into a friggin' masterpiece. If you're not convinced, do yourself a favor and open up Youtube. Look up "Thousand March (War)," "Unexpectancy Phase 3" (mind that you click just a pure audio version, as this otherwise spoils the final boss), "Oregano Mirage" and "Tropical Crust" for a good variety of music leaning towards varying styles, but all of them delivering. This is the first soundtrack I've heard in I don't know how long where I struggle to name a song I didn't enjoy. This is one of those soundtracks you buy AFTER buying the game simply out of principle of supporting the music.

-A good balance between difficulties for more casual players and people looking for a challenge and something new to master. Each level has a letter grade, and "the Good Ending" can be unlocked simply by finding all secret ingredients, and does not require full 100% mastery. Likewise, a letter grade of A feels entirely feasible; I've gotten them multiple times when I felt I was playing bad. To get the elusive P-ranks though, one needs to get every secret and ingredient a level has in the same run, and you cannot drop your kill combo, which itself must be started in room 1 of the level. This effectively means you need to kill an enemy or grab something with a point value every ~3 seconds or the P-rank is lost. It's still forgiving enough that you're allowed to get hit and take damage, but a hit easily shaves a full second off your timer til the next kill. P-rank strikes a nice balance between being feasible (A Hat in Time for example sometimes felt absolutely brutal with it's Death Wishes, as if that part of the DLC was absolutely catered to the top 0.1% of speedrunners), whilst still being challenging and rewarding.

-The art style, while I could understand why it might look poor or off-putting to some, will grow on you incredibly quickly. I was neutral about it but have come to really appreciate it. It really fits the mood the game was going for, and it's always nice to see hand-crafted art that dares to do something stylistic instead of just copypasting the most popular art style of the era. 

Peppino is also surprisingly expressive in a good way. For example, I love getting killstreaks in Team Fortress 2 with Scout in particular, because Scout will start trashtalking opponents real hard, which just suits the mood one feels when they know they're on fire and in the opponent's head. Peppino will similarly start levels timid and nervous, but as a combo builds and the score climbs, he becomes more headstrong and aggressive, even aggressively dancing in place or breathing heavily like an angered thug when idle.

I fully recommend this purchase for any speed junkies out there who want their adrenaline pumping. My only frustration with it is I'm a perfectionist who has to "prove" I can overcome any challenges, and now this game's got me bunkering down to get all those P-ranks lol. (That's on me though, obviously)

This is my first review for the first game I ever bought on Steam, so I apologize if there's some mistakes here and there.

This game is about the fat, fast and furious pizza man known as Peppino Spaghetti, on his mission to protect his establishment from being destroyed by a sentient flying pizza...yup.

This game is clearly inspired by other games, such as Sonic and Wario Land, focusing on getting as many points as possible while also going very fast, a very simple premise that is very well executed.

Explore the levels, beat every enemy you see and destroy the pillar at the end to start a timer, you now have to leave by doing the level in reverse, and if you have the courage, you can try for a Lap 2, whitin the same time limit you have to do the whole level in reverse yet again.

With all that out of the way, let's go for the Pros and Cons.

Pros:

- The graphics are fantastic, everything fells like it was made on MS Paint, giving the vibes of old cartoons, every single thing that moves has so many frames of animations, I think Peppino himself has more than 1000 frames, with most of those sadly going unused.

- The music is even better, every single song is either good or amazing, with my personal favorites being It's Pizza Time!, Tropical Crust, Extraterrestial Wahwahs, Tubular Trash Zone, Thousand March, Unexpectancy, and specially, There's a Bone in my Spaghetti. Even if you don't care at all about this game, please, at the very least listen to the soundtrack, it's fantastic.

- Both Peppino and Noise are very smooth to control, it takes some time to get used to it, specially the Noise, but after you get the hang of it, it feels really satisfying to go Mach 4 and just fly through levels. And the transformations feel unique and makes every level feel pretty different from one another.

- P ranking feels very satifying, beat the entire level in one combo while getting every collectable and finding every secret while also having to do the 2nd Lap. Even if you fail, it doesn't suck to try again since the characters control so well and you can go so fast. 

With all that said, the game is not perfect, and there's some design issues that I have that could be improved upon.

Cons:

- The tutorial for the game gets the job done, but a lot of additional info is told by Pizza Granny, in random locations throughout the tower, which makes them very easy to miss, there are 2 secrets in the game that have notes made by said character telling what you should do, I feel like there could be more in other stages, in particular on Bloodsauce Dungeon, speaking of which...

- Bloodsauce Dungeon, this is a large difficult spike compared to the other levels of the first floor, you can barely go Mach 4 since it focuses too much on verticality, and Peppino isn't really good at that, specially while having to go downwards, combine that with the fact that you don't know right away that it's possible to cancel a Dive into a Body Slam and this becomes a hard level that is introduced wayyy to early in the game, it should have been replaced with Wasteyard, so Bloodsauce could go into the second floor instead.

- The game focuses a lot on getting the P rank, but not only is the explanation not perfect, and yet again missable since a random Pizza Granny tells you about it, but you can't even see what is the amount of points necessary for it, on a game that focuses on score attack, it's a very weird thing to miss. Not to mention that finding Gerome and the Secret Door is really hard in some levels. I think that fully paying Mr. Stick should reward the player with a radar or detector to give an idea to player if they are close to the secrets or not.

- Fake Peppino is a badly designed boss fight. Pepperman is easy but at least it's quick, Vigilante is gimmicky but after you get the hang of it he can be easily defeated, The Noise is the best fight in the game, the Final Boss takes a bit too long but the presentation is so well done that it makes up for it.
And then we have Fake Peppino with multiple problems:

> He takes 3 entire hits for his HP to go down, making it a total of 36 hits, that is way too much and makes the fight go on for longer than necessary.

> His attacks on the first phase not only take forever to finish, they're also a joke to avoid, one of them can be avoided by just *standing still*...and said attack also lasts for 10 seconds... why?

> It's very hard to tell if he can be damaged or not, the other bosses start flashing with a unique sound effect, make it very clear that you can hit them, Fake Pep on the other hand only does that after every 2 hits, where he's left stunned forever when it's very obvious that he can get hit. 

Combine all of that and even on my best attempts he ends up taking more than 3 minutes to defeat, when other bosses have much better pacing and only take a little more than 2 minutes. This boss is a chore to P Rank.

Conclusion:

Despite its flaws, it's a fantastic experience and I don't regret buying this game at all, the great Artstyle, Music and Gameplay more than makes up for it. There's not much for people that just wanna finish the levels and defeat the final boss, but if you go out of your way to get the elusive P Rank, you will be in for a ride.

My final score is a 9/10, very good game, and I'm excited to see what the developers will do for their next game Woon.

I don't like platformers. Something about them has always made them unenjoyable to play through for me. Whether it be the clunky controls or constant repetition in common IP platformers nowadays, I don't know. Pizza Tower managed to flip my whole predisposition about platformers.

The story is not a major part of this game, but its addition just adds a slight bit of charm that makes it just a bit more enjoyable to play. Essentially, you're a failing pizza restaurant owner, Peppino, and while minding your own business you're approached by Pizzaface, who threatens to blow your store up with a laser shot from the top of his Pizza Tower. Peppino races towards the top of the tower to stop his store's inevitable demise. Bosses don't really contribute to this story (except for maybe the 4th and 5th) but the implication that you're knocking down 'employees' left and right to make your way to the top is enjoyable.

The whole movement in this game is based on three keys, excluding the movement keys. You have one key for dashing, one for jumping, and one for running. All of these combine into an extremely fluid and expansive moveset that allows for so many options when traversing through the detailed and diverse geometry. The game has also been built perfectly to be as speedrunn-able as possible, with every action that Peppino makes being as reactive as possible, and you can even stall your movement momentarily by pressing the taunt key!

The levels include some of the most creative environments and mechanics that I have ever seen in a platformer. Like I mentioned in the start, a big annoyance for me in platformers is the constant repetition, parts and mechanics being constantly reused with very little attempt made to change their interactions with the levels. Pizza Tower pretty much introduces a handful of mechanics on every single level, of which there are 19. Most of these mechanics are transformations, things that completely change the way Peppino works, and it's a pleasant addition, as you don't have Peppino's main moveset for the entire duration of the game. Other mechanics are minuscule things that become a mainstay after they have been introduced, like speed boosters, or conveyor belts, which don't initially show in the tutorial. The constant additions allow the game to remain fresh all the way to the end.

The bosses are like this too. Half of the bosses follow the conventional "invincible until they're not" and the other half let you attack all the time. Each and every boss in this game is unique. They all have their own personality, moveset, and ending move. Each boss has two phases, and after you deplete their health fully, you are given a last chance to finish them off before they regenerate one HP. Each of these finishing moves is different from boss to boss, and they all tie in to the boss's theming. Similarly to the levels, each boss feels fresh and you pretty much never know what you're getting into when you fight them.

"Pizza Time" is what I would call the main twist of this game. When you get to the end of a level, you destroy John Pillar, and suddenly a timer activates where you need to get back to the start of the level before time runs out. Every level is made to work just as well backwards, and paths will often close and open up, not only enabling a speedier exit, but also allowing for different and new things to happen even during Pizza Time. If you've beaten a level already, and you're in Pizza Time, there will be a portal near the exit that will teleport you back to where you activated Pizza Time in the first place. That whole interaction will cause Lap 2 to begin, which is a risky choice that involves doing the entire escape sequence again while keeping the same timer you had when entering the portal. Doing this is a fun extra challenge for people to see how fast they can possibly go, but can also increase your combo counter, or score.

Replayability is a strong suit for this game. The amount of unique achievements allow users to be able to replay levels with a small shift and still be fun to achieve. There are also clothing, which is a type of customisation which allows players to change the colours or patterns of Peppino's outfit with a fun array of unique ways to get them. Lastly, the ranking system, which will determine how well you did in a level with a letter grade, from D to A, then S, and then P. You can't really get an S rank without doing the second lap, And you can't get a P rank without doing everything for a rank S, and then getting every secret in a level, a level's unique tower treasure, while also not dropping a combo for the entire level. The inclusion of the P rank was very smart, and it enables a lot of extra mileage for the game where pulling it off is not only very challenging but very relieving and rewarding.

If you know about Pizza Tower, there's a good chance you know the soundtrack, which is a masterful composition of possibly some of the best VGM's I've heard in a very long time. The majority of the tracks are composed using samples of various types, from voice samples to Gameboy instrument samples, it's all here, and it all works so well together. There are a few tracks in here too with some superb guitar. This isn't a review of the OST, but all the tracks work so perfectly with what's happening on the screen. No track will really get repeated except for "It's Pizza Time" and "The Death I Deservioli" which are both escape themes and are made so well that it does not get boring listening to them for the thousandth time while trying to get a P rank on some really hard level. Some of my favourites are "Oregano Mirage", "Wudpecker" and "There's A Bone In My Spaghetti!". Each of them are wonderful to listen on their own, but it works so well with all the sound effects in-game.

All this and 5 years of development pulls together in what can truly be called a masterpiece. Its unconventional style leads it on with a ton of identity and extremely fun gameplay. I hope Pizza Tower remains to be a mainstay in the gaming community, and that it's deserved praise continues.

PIZZA TOWER is a love letter to game design, art, and music in tandem. It truly is riddled with charm, chaos, wild mechanics, and super cheesy animation. This game really does have it all. In the afterglow of playing it, I have trouble thinking of anything to criticize.

  For working adults, it's the perfect get-away for the weekend. The time it takes to actually complete the game is not very long, yet has a massive replay-ability, even on terms of level to level basis. With the concept of the game being reminiscent to old school platformers like Warioland, I hate making that comparison because they are remarkably different experiences. 

  I think this game may have some learning curves for casual players; The challenges are more difficult than most Nintendo games, but not near as hard as say, Cuphead. Boss levels, for example, change up the move set preformed to keep the actions interesting and not "too predictable", but I think they are simple enough to learn how to maneuver, once you've seen them once or twice. 

  That being said, learning how to Master this game is where it really shines.
  Learning how to master Pizza Tower is no easy task, and a speedrunner's dream. Precision platforming with many ways to tackle the world, with the ability to go at super speeds truly gives a sense of being unstoppable when you grasp it at its full potential and go barreling through a level like a force of nature.

  As an animator, I was laughing at every single pose. Every button press, every enemy reaction, every cutscene, Pizza tower literally had me hollering. It reminds me of why I wanted to be an artist in the first place- to bring people joy in such a tactful way. I cannot recommend this game enough for what it is, and continues to be. Its popularity is massive for a reason.

  I highly recommend this game, and think everybody whom chooses to dive into it will find something to love about it.

Pizza Tower is the only 2D platformer I have ever played and truly, holistically, personally liked. I can respect Mario and Sonic's catalogs, and smaller games like Fancy Pants's games and Super Meat Boy, but I genuinely like Pizza Tower for myself, by myself, because it's awesome in basically every major department I can think of. I don't just like this game, I *love* it. Like-- seriously, I don't know where to start.

As I've gotten older, my standards in/for the games I've played have gotten higher and higher, while still being picky about things like difficulty, control, and presentation. Every time I go back to 2D Sonic these days (with the exception of maybe Mania), I'm absolutely barraged by mental notes while playing; about how I'd do this mechanic differently, about how this part of level design was poorly implemented, about how this boss feels like it was designed in an hour, and on and on and on. It adds up fast, and while it doesn't *ruin* these games by any means, it does dent my enjoyment of them significantly. With Pizza Tower, I think my one and only major complaint is that there's not *more*. Some kind of museum to play the game's many demos and learn more about them, more playable characters, more levels - that sort of thing. 

Pizza Tower is incredible. It makes Sonic nearly obsolete and feels like the angel sent to earth just for me, after years of languishing alone, as someone who was never really able to get into Mario ever despite trying. An extremely fast, tightly-controlling platformer that's nearly nonstop, balls-to-the-wall adrenaline combined with the smarts and reaction speed to channel that adrenaline productively; set to a visual, tonal and sonical energy that's every part as it's unique as it is VERY appealing. This game isn't somehow *incredibly badass* feeling to play in spite of it being goofy ahh, but precisely BECAUSE it is, owning the MS Paint-meets-Boomerang wholeheartedly without overdoing it to the point of making the humor feel forced.

This game uses the same tricks to encourage the player to get better while rarely forcing them that fucking *Ultrakill* does. Most of this game's collectables do nothing but make a completion value go up, but you still want to earn them, because figuring out how to find and get them often goes hand-in-hand with learning how to do the levels faster and get those elusive S- or even P-ranks. Taking a Wario Land style 2D platformer about learning a level forwards, then having to speedrun it backwards, and cranking up the speed by a factor of *three* is one thing; giving it some of the best level design and artistic presentation imaginable is another; but then challenging the player to get everything in that level AND THEN GO ALL THE WAY BACK AROUND AGAIN WITH ONLY THE TIME LEFT YOU LEAVE YOURSELF DURING THE *FIRST* ESCAPE SEQUENCE IN ORDER TO GET 100% COMPLETION FOR THAT LEVEL is SO PSYCHOTIC that it should not work, but it does. It's IN the game, it's HOW Pizza Tower works. In its stupid, goofy, cartoony way, it dares you to be badass.

Also, I don't know how else to fit it in this review, but the boss fights are also perfect?? Instead of being pseudo-levels that don't deserve the designation of "boss fight", or nothingburgers that are just included out of game-trope obligation, Pizza Tower's boss fights are ALSO INCREDIBLE. You get locked in a one-screen-sized box with one of five extremely distinctively-fighting opponents and are challeneged to not just beat them, but style on them as hard as possible by minimizing the damage you take, while they all try *as hard as possible* to stop you from doing either. While Pepperman and The Noise involve a fair amount of waiting for an attack to end, then countering, even they put engaging and highly energized spins on the concepts. The Vigilante and the fourth boss, on the other hand, are genuinely some of the best boss fights I've fought in ANY game, being insanely chaotic yet perfectly balanced games of back-and-forth where you and your opponent both always looking for an opening, then doing everything you can to exploit it once found; the Vigilante especially is so *absolutely sensational* that it makes me even more upset that the ability to play as him was scrapped.

All of this, by the way is wrapped up in - as *insane* or uninformed as this is going to sound - what I consider to be my absolute, #1 game soundtrack of all time. No other game I've ever played across any genre has had this level of cohesion, quality, sauce, vision, and pure *awesomeness* as Pizza Tower's soundtrack. There isn't a single level or boss track I skip when going back for a relisten or making a playlist, and even the menu and hub-world themes have their appeal. It's incredible, it's INSANE, this game's music ALONE bumps it up a letter grade it's so good and that's on top of this game being an A+ at minimum already. It's ILLEGAL. 

Again, my only gripe is that, while the content present is alone worth over twice the $20 price - you get everything in the base game with Peppino, a New Game+ with The Noise (who handles differently and has modified levels, scenarios, a unique boss fight, and multiple new pieces of music), and a secret co-op *New Game ++* where either you can play as both at once, or you and a friend can control them individually with unique combination moves - there should have been more. Mods have already added all the bosses as playable characters with all their own flair - including the ones the developers themselves have said would take too much effort - and experiencing PIzza Tower's *wealth* of fascinating development history requires going outside the game, when some kind of museum showing it all - and potentially even letting players play some of them - would be an amazing show of sportsmanship in the realm of teaching game development, and providing game preservation.

You should play this game. Even if you don't like games like Pizza Tower. Please. Genuine, wholehearted near-perfect games like these are so, so, rare.

Let me get one thing out of the way: I never actually played any of the Wario Land games before, so whether or not this game succeeds in being a spiritual successor to that series, I can't say. What I CAN say is that Pizza Tower may be one of, if not the best platformers I've played in such a very long time. I don't think I've ever experienced a game so tightly woven together like this one.

You play as Peppino, a very angry and anxiety-induced pizza man, on a journey to keep his pizza business from falling into debt by running through a tower filled with dangerous and quirky stages. Or at least, that's the interpretation I got from the opening intro. Really, the narrative isn't a super strong point here, but that doesn't really matter. All you need to know is this game's aesthetics harkens back to the old school, squigly-style cartoons of the 90's/early 2000's, like Ren and Stimpy, Ed, Edd and Eddy and Cow & Chicken, and the humor is a definite match of those cartoons as well. But don't let that fool you: the gameplay and controls for this game are NO JOKE. Peppino's movement is phenomenal. Super tight with a lot of cool techniques to give yourself a plethora of ways of maneuvering around the stages. You got the basics, like dashing forward, jumping, wallrunning. You got some advanced movements like sliding, shinesparking, diving. And then you got the straight up advanced techs like dive cancel stomps, grab cancels, slide boosting. All of these can be strung together in order to keep control of Peppino as you make a mad dash for the goal. It all lends itself to a true speedrunner's dream, because if you string it all perfectly together, the speed becomes hella exhilarating. Ludicrous even (sadly there is no plaid costume for your character).

Unlike most typical platformers, stages aren't designed with the typical "Point A to Point B" layout. Instead, each stage has you running through a huge, maze-like arena, figuring out the best path to get to the goal. Once you reach your goal, you are then tasked to make it back to the starting point as fast as you can, as you are given a time limit to do so. Run out of time and you'll start to be chased by the evil Pizza Face. Get caught before you reach the beginning and it's game over. BUT THAT'S NOT ALL. If you're feeling daring, you can partake in a lap 2 just as you reach the starting point, in which case you're tasked with running through the map AGAIN with the remaining time left. If you're able to keep your combo meter going by picking up items and attacking enemies with very little breather in-between as you make your way all across lap, you might just get the ever elusive "P" rank, to showcase your amazing Pizza skills.

None of the stages in this game were ever bad. They were all so perfectly designed, I felt compelled to P rank every single one of them before even getting to the end game. Some stages had gimmicks, like picking up a shotgun in order to shoot down indestructable walls, grabbing a rocket in order to boost across the air, turning into a pizza box in order to flap across areas in a single bound. These gimmicks never felt tacked on; they all felt like a good mix up to the overall flow of the game. If I could make one complaint here, it's the fact that there is SO MUCH cut content for this game. I followed this game's development from the day it had its SAGE demo uploaded all the way to now. It's quite sad to see a lot of cool stuff get dummied out, but I guess that's also what helped make the game feel so tight so I can understand the choices the devs made in having to remove a lot of stuff, so if nothing else, it just means there's potential for DLC stuff. If that doesn't happen, it's not the end of the world, because this game is pretty much Pizza Perfect.

Also, special shout outs to the music. It's super stylish. It's kinda hard to explain, but the best way I can do so is imagine if the OST of Sonic CD, Earthworm Jim and Jet Set Radio were all thrown into a blender spinning atop a turntable. The music just oozes style, from the sick hip hop beats of the pause music making you wanna break it down, to the frenetic electronic jam as you're dashing through lap 2 which further adds to the adrenaline rush of the experience. I'm telling you, if you put on a pair of headphones and play "The Death That I Deservioli" while going out for a jog, expect to find yourself a million miles away from home. It's THAT wild.

This game is really good. If you love high speed platformers or just enjoy speedrunning, this is the perfect entry on the menu. So make sure to order it with extra cheese, and don't you dare save room for dessert.

[h1]Pizza Tower is a delectable delight.[/h1]
I have very little experience with the Wario Land series. The only game I ever played from that lineup was Shake It when I was really young and I have mixed memories of it. I only really liked the animated cutscenes as a kid and I found the gameplay to be really slow. Fortunately for Pizza Tower, I can describe this game as the exact opposite. I rarely go out of my way to experience every single detail a game offers. But in this case, I soaked almost 60 hours into 100%-ing Pizza Tower and I had fun every second of the way.

For those who have absolutely no experience with the Wario Land games, it plays like your standard 2D platformer collectathon at the absolute basics. You walk around through a level to get all the pizza toppings you need and at the end, you do your best to escape before time runs out. Running all the way back to the start of the level in any other game would be a chore, but Pizza Tower executes it well enough that you often won’t retread familiar ground. And even when you do, the layout is drastically different when you’re coming from a different direction. Describing the game’s level design as phenomenal is an understatement. Not only are the levels designed with your retreat in mind, but they also have unique mechanics tied to them. Every level has its own power-up to offer you. You’ll turn into a fire tornado in one level and have a literal shotgun in another level. Even levels that would seem incredibly gimmicky like the Golf! level flow incredibly naturally because you can just run at top speed and hit the ball that way. There is not a single level that I ended up hating and every level offered a drastically different experience. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2975129880
Amazing level design alone is something that really sells me on a game. But Pizza Tower doesn’t just take influence from the Wario Land series. I would argue that Peppino moves much faster than Sonic did in the Genesis games. You’re also given a lot more opportunities to move at top speeds for both low-level and high-level play. You will storm through enemies so quickly, they stop and scream at the sight of you. Peppino’s moveset may seem simple on the surface, but he’s got a few tricks under-the-hood. Most players won’t immediately realize the taunt doubles not only as a parry but as a screen-clearing ultimate attack. There are other moves that you’ll have to figure out on your own like the uppercut and quick ground pound, along with some other techniques you can pull off to reach top speed even faster. Pizza Tower has something to offer to the most diehard fans of 2D platformers and for those who absolutely suck at them. Going for a P-Rank was one of the most enjoyable challenges a game has offered me. Some of them took several attempts but never did I ever think that I was unrightfully robbed of earning one. I highly suggest aiming for a few, even if you don’t plan on snagging them all. But what if you’re really bad at the game? It’s still worth picking up because the only way you can actually fail at Pizza Tower is by getting caught in the escape sequence when time runs out. While new players may struggle with quickly moving around, they’ll usually have enough time because you’re meant to have time for a second lap. Otherwise, Peppino is completely invincible. Getting hurt by an enemy or falling in a bit may cause you to lose your combo or a bit of score, but it’s nothing major. I would personally encourage practicing for the harder content the game offers because it’s both fair and challenging. With enough time and effort, anyone can do it.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2975129747 
Also, this game has one of the best soundtracks hands down. I have frequently listened to it even after finishing the game. Every level and boss has at least 1 unique song to accompany it, with some having 2 or more. As a result, the soundtrack is incredibly varied. You’ve got a tropical groove with Crust Cove’s song, calm and relaxing tunes like the one found in the refrigerator level, extremely goofy songs like Good Eatin’, interstellar bops like Extraterrestrial Wahwahs, and many more. There’s not a single track I dislike in the entire game. And nothing compares to the sheer level of anxiety that It’s Pizza Time will induce in you. I didn’t have a problem with there being only 1 escape theme. It’s the song that convinced me to buy the game. That song just inflicts a level of urgency in me no matter what I’m doing and I absolutely love it. If this game isn’t recognized for its stunning soundtrack in the Game Awards or Steam Awards, I will be greatly upset. I could sit on the main menu alone and listen to that song for hours. If you’re a fan of when game soundtracks sample sounds, I think you’ll especially like this game’s soundtrack. I recognized a few from Jet Set Radio and Sonic CD personally. 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B7gGacb8cO4
The artwork is another highlight. It gives off huge 90’s cartoon vibes with its fluent animation and goofy character designs. There’s even some gross-out art that a lot of cartoons used at a point in the game. Peppino has a lot of potential reactions to the world around him. Every move you make, power-up you take, and enemy you get hit by will have a silly art piece/animation of Peppino to accompany it. Each level has a unique title card and that’s where my small complaints with the art direction lie. Most of them look more than fine, but some of them I can just tell they were drawn in MS Paint and it really shows. Again, there are only like 3 standouts like that in the 2 dozen levels, but it sticks out in a gem like this. Otherwise, Pizza Tower looks great. I particularly liked how ridiculous they got with the pizza theme at some points. The mere existence of The Noise as a boss is something so out there, I adore that they did it. There’s another level towards the end that you wouldn’t expect that fits perfectly with the food theme. It is absurd how far the developers were able to carry a pizza theme and I promise it doesn’t end at what kind of toppings you would use.

Pizza Tower was such a treat to play through. This is usually the point where I would go over a huge problem that I had with the game, but my complaints are so minuscule that I can’t describe them past a sentence. The fact that reloading the game starts you at the beginning of the hub is slightly annoying, but that’s it. Basically, the only other thing anyone could be upset over is that there isn’t really a story, but I know plenty of people who don’t even care that the game doesn’t offer one. This game was so much fun. There wasn’t a point where I was bored and frustrated, but there were several incredibly euphoric moments while I was snagging the P-Ranks.  A normal first-time playthrough will take you around 6 or so hours, but you can get a lot of time by doing everything. Just look at my hour count at the time of this review. [b]I am giving Pizza Tower a 9/10 as my final score. It just shows when you have passion for a project combined with letting it have enough time in the oven, that you come out with an amazing game.[/b]

If you'd asked me for my thoughts on Pizza Tower after my first hour or two, you'd have been met with a frustrated "I can see why people like it, but this isn't for me". It's a good thing, then, that I kept playing for a total of 45 hours before posting my thoughts, because after P-ranking every level in the game and achieving 101% completion, I am wholly and utterly convinced that this is one of the best platformers ever made.

Most of that frustration, I think, stemmed from a dissonance or clash with my beliefs - One of which is "I am good at platformers and speedrun games". I've always considered myself very good at both of these genres. But I was [i]extremely[/i] humbled by Pizza Tower at first.
Using Super Meat Boy as a comparison (as it's both a renowned 'difficult game' and 'go fast 2D platformer'), the difficulty comes from the level design, obstacle and enemy placement, stuff like that - But Pizza Tower's [i]very fundamentals[/i] are hard. Even just the simple act of moving fast, with precision, is hard at first here - I found myself slamming into walls and losing momentum, unable to maintain any kind of combo on enemies, and just generally sort of fumbling through. I was struggling basically instantly.
This game, in my experience, is not beginner friendly in the least. It speaks a complex tongue, and doesn't care all too much about helping the player to understand and speak it's language.
It only gets away with this because there is SO much depth in every facet of Peppino's movement. His suite of abilities is extremely versatile, and if you want to chase the highest ranks, it demands that you truly learn and understand not just how those abilities work, but how and where you should apply them, and think outside the box to understand how to use the tools it gives you. 
In this way, Pizza Tower asks a lot of you - More than most games, even the ones that are renowned as being difficult (Super Meat Boy once again comes to mind).

It's a shame that so many people will be filtered by the steep learning curve, because there's something really special in here - You just might need to dig a little to find it. This is a fantastic, tightly designed, extremely fun platformer.

A big part of said learning curve revealed itself to me as I started to chase down P-ranks - Most precision platformers such as Super Meat Boy only ever demand 45-60 seconds of perfection from you at a time (and those would be considered to be on the longer side for that game). Pizza Tower doesn't [i]quite[/i] demand the same level of perfection - you're allowed to make mistakes and even take damage as long as you can recover quickly enough not to drop your combo - but you're regularly asked to keep up this high standard of performance for 6-8 minutes per run. There's a lot to be said for how difficult this can be. Six minutes is a [i]long[/i] time when you're moving at lightspeed and aren't allowed to drop your combo even once.

The levels are all super varied, with almost every level having a unique gimmick or mechanic in it that continued to surprise and delight as I made progress. One level has you transforming into a ghost, allowing you to pass through certain walls into new areas. Another level bakes [i]golfing[/i] into the platforming design, complete with par scores for each hole. There's one that just gives you a shotgun and says 'yeah, go nuts'. These all put a smile on my face the first time I saw them. Pizza Tower would have already been great without these, thanks to it's strong level design, unhinged graphical style and banger soundtrack - they didn't need to go so hard, but they did it for us, and the game is all the better for it.

Pizza Tower is one of those games that can give you a completely different impression depending on how you choose to play it.

If you simply want to reach the ending, it is a good, weird, energetic platformer that is honestly not particularly difficult. You run through bizarre levels, smash everything in your path, fight some bosses, listen to excellent music and eventually finish the game.

And if that is all you do, I can actually understand someone walking away wondering why people praise Pizza Tower so much.

The game truly reveals itself when you decide to get P-ranks.

But first, let's get something out of the way: Pizza Tower owes an enormous amount to Wario Land, especially Wario Land 4.

I used to associate Pizza Tower much more with Sonic because of its speed, momentum and the process of learning a level until you can fly through it almost without stopping. After actually looking at Wario Land gameplay, though... yeah. Nintendo deserves a lot of credit for the skeleton here. Transformations, smashing through enemies and obstacles instead of carefully jumping on them, the structure of entering a level and later escaping from it, the general physicality of the protagonist — Pizza Tower takes an incredible amount from Wario.

What Pizza Tower does with that foundation is effectively turn Wario Land into a speed game.

Peppino has a fantastic moveset. Once you build momentum, you can charge through enemies, run up walls, dive, slide, grab things, chain actions together and generally turn yourself into a screaming Italian projectile.

There is also the taunt, which doubles as a parry and gives Peppino another defensive option, but the most important addition is simply how strongly the entire game is built around maintaining movement.

This is where the Sonic comparison still makes sense to me.

The goal eventually stops being merely reaching the end of the level. You learn the route. You learn where you can preserve speed, which movement transitions are faster, where collectibles are located and how to move through the entire stage as one continuous sequence instead of a collection of individual platforming challenges.

And this is also why I disagree with people describing Pizza Time as annoying backtracking.

I am not even sure I would call it backtracking.

A level effectively has two endpoints: the entrance and the pillar you destroy to start Pizza Time. But the route from the pillar back to the exit is not simply the same level played backwards.

Sometimes you briefly travel through mirrored pieces of terrain, sure, but in the context of the whole escape route that is a tiny part of the experience. The return trip is designed as its own track.

When you destroy the pillar, you are not really returning to the beginning of the level.

You are continuing toward its actual ending.

That distinction matters because Pizza Time is one of the reasons these levels work so well. You first experience the stage at a relatively normal pace, learn its gimmicks and layout, and then the game effectively says:

"Good. Now run."

And the geometry suddenly makes sense in a different way.

The other major thing Pizza Tower does extremely well is making individual stages memorable.

Almost every level has its own theme, visual joke or reference. Cowboys, a farm, Vietnam, aliens, pirates, movies, robots, FNAF-style horror and a ridiculous number of other ideas appear throughout the game.

But the important part is that these are not just background changes.

Most levels also introduce some kind of transformation or temporary mechanical gimmick that changes how Peppino moves or interacts with the stage. The transformation only lasts for a portion of the level, but you usually have to understand and use it properly to progress.

That means stages are remembered not only because they looked different or had different music, but because they actually played differently for a while.

This variety is one of the reasons Pizza Tower rarely feels repetitive despite asking you to replay levels.

And you WILL replay them if you go for P-ranks.

This is where the game goes from "good platformer" to something much more impressive.

Getting through a stage normally does not require you to master Peppino's movement. You can make mistakes, stop, look around, take damage and generally brute-force your way through most situations.

P-rank completely changes your relationship with the level.

Now you need to understand the route.

You need to collect everything required.

You need to keep your combo alive.

You need to avoid unnecessary interruptions.

You need to use Peppino's moveset properly instead of treating half of it as optional tricks.

Eventually you stop thinking about individual rooms and start thinking about the level as one continuous route.

And this is where the level design becomes fucking impressive.

Sections that seemed like random platforms during your first run suddenly reveal themselves as perfectly placed transitions between moves. Obstacles that originally slowed you down become things you learn to destroy without losing momentum. You begin planning how to enter a room before you even reach it because you already know how you want to leave it.

At that point Pizza Tower starts giving you something very close to a speedrunning experience without requiring you to actually become a competitive speedrunner.

You are routing the stage.

You are shaving off unnecessary movement.

You are learning how to maintain momentum.

You are restarting after tiny mistakes because you know you can do better.

And finally getting the P-rank feels good not because the game gave you better equipment, more damage or a higher level.

You got better.

That is probably the single most important thing Pizza Tower does right.

Its progression at the highest level is primarily player progression.

The music deserves its own paragraph because it carries an absurd amount of this experience.

Pizza Tower's soundtrack is a chaotic mixture of electronic music, samples, strange noises and melodies that somehow perfectly match the game's manic energy.

It is fantastic.

And this matters mechanically more than it might sound.

When you are attempting the same P-rank again and again, restarting a stage stops being nearly as painful when you are listening to music this good.

Pizza Time themes turn an already fast platformer into controlled panic.

Boss themes are arguably even better.

Honestly, some of the strongest music in the game appears during boss fights.

Which is funny, because bosses are one area where my opinion became less positive the better I became at the game.

During a normal first playthrough, bosses are great.

They are expressive, funny, visually memorable and each has its own gimmicks. At that point they can easily seem like some of the best parts of Pizza Tower.

But mechanically, most of them can eventually be simplified into something like:

dodge
dodge
dodge
attack

Repeat.

Obviously that is a simplification, but the point is that their movesets are not particularly deep.

And the P-rank requirement exposes that limitation.

Normal levels become MORE interesting when you chase P-ranks because the requirement forces you to fully engage with the movement system and level design.

Bosses have almost the opposite problem.

Chasing their P-ranks effectively turns them into no-hit fights.

I thought I would like this game, I wanted to like this game, but I didn’t like this game and I don’t really think it’s the game’s fault I didn’t like it.

 The main thing was that there were two separate incentives to the game that were at odds with each other that just really stopped the game from ‘clicking’ for me. All of the mechanics seemed to be designed to push the player to go fast and reckless to push the combo meter as high as they could (and it was more fun to play that way). However, all the rewards seemed to more heavily incentivize being slow and methodical, checking every corner for secrets. In fact, much of the progression was linked to exploring a level thoroughly to find certain key items and I had difficulty enjoying the slow search when every fiber of my being just wanted to crash through everything.

The humor also didn’t really “click” for me. I know there are people out there who really enjoy some random chaos, but for me it felt like I was playing in the vibe of a joke without a punchline.

Overall, I think this game accomplishes what it set out to do and I can see why a lot of people enjoy it, but I really wish I had thought more deeply about whether this was actually a game for me before getting swept along in the hype.

With Nintendo having neglected the amazing Wario Land series since 2008's Shake It, it was up to the fans to fill in the gaps. Behold, a game that's gone through 4 long years of development, Pizza Tower! Most heavily inspired by Wario Land 4, but animated beautifully in the style of 90's cartoons, Pizza Tower is already one of the best 2D platformers I've ever played. Beautifully deranged shit-post on the outside, stellar action platformer on the inside.

It’s really hard to find a fault in Pizza Tower. As hard as I try, I can only think of minor nitpicks. This game does everything right when it comes to providing a premier speed platforming experience.

Controls might require some time to adjust, but that’s just because character’s movements simulate inertia of an overweight middle-aged Italian acting as a freight train… with scientific precision. Your options for tacking obstacles are plenty and thanks to stellar animations and sound design, you can feel every jump, every mile-per-hour running and every enemy pulverized on your path.

Level design is also near flawless. Stages not only burst with style and creativity, but also provide tons of gimmicks and transformations that spice your gameplay - like chili pepper and oregano on your usual Diavola pizza. I would be hard pressed to find level geometry that doesn’t go well with flow of the controls. Readability of obstacles, enemies and collectibles is crystal clear. So clear are also boss patterns – a secret ingredient that makes occasional battles fun and challenging.

Presentation speaks for itself. I can understand if it’s not somebody’s cup of tea, but artstyle’s insanity is intoxicating. It might look ugly at first, but paradoxically, it feels surprisingly cohesive. Pizza Tower’s world feels seamless and you have no trouble immersing yourself into its embrace. Soundtrack also helps on that front by being genuine funky bangers all around. 

For the aforementioned nitpicks - I am really gasping for straws here. I guess tutorials for characters could be more elegant and less frontload with information? Controls are also a little less fine tuned for secret hunting than speedy traversal. This might be a problem at the very start, but after you get used to it – it’s not a big hurdle.

Pizza Tower is not especially difficult to just beat, but it does provide a tough but very fair challenge in form of P Ranks. Those can bump your 5-6 hours playthrough to far bigger numbers. I would definitely recommend sticking to the game until 100% completion – not for a prize, but for a hard but very rewarding experience.
